On the other side: a human body. A human life. A person who, whatever their failings, whatever their crimes, possesses the same nervous system you do — the same capacity to feel agony, the same fragile skull, the same family who would grieve over their broken body.

And we are asked to believe these two sides balance?

They do not balance. They have never balanced. And no civilization worthy of the name has ever truly believed they do.

Let me take you on a brief journey through history.

There was a time when a man could be hanged for stealing a loaf of bread. There was a time when a child could be transported to a penal colony for pickpocketing a handkerchief. There was a time when a plantation owner could whip, maim, or kill to protect what the law called his "property" — including other human beings.

We look back on these eras and we shudder. We call them barbaric. We say, "We have evolved beyond that."

But have we?

When we argue that a person is justified in using lethal force to stop someone from stealing their car — not threatening their life, not endangering their family, just taking their car — how far have we really come from the gallows built for bread thieves?

The principle is the same: that material possessions are worth more than human wholeness. We have simply dressed it in different language.

Now, some will say to me — and I welcome the challenge — "But if we don't meet theft with force, we invite chaos. We invite a world where nothing is safe, where criminals run rampant, where the law-abiding are victims."

I understand this fear. I respect this fear. But I reject its conclusion.

Because we do not live in a world without alternatives. We have locks. We have alarms. We have surveillance. We have insurance. We have law enforcement. We have courts. We have community watch programs. We have a vast and sophisticated infrastructure designed precisely to address theft without requiring individual citizens to become judge, jury, and executioner over a stolen laptop.

Violence in defense of property is not our only option. It is our laziest option. It is our most dangerous option. And it is our most morally corrosive option.

Because here is what the advocates of property violence never want to discuss: the practical consequences.

What happens when we normalize violence in defense of things?

Mistakes happen. A teenager cuts through your yard at night — is he a burglar or is he taking a shortcut home? A neighbor enters your garage thinking it's a community sale. A child chases a ball onto your property. A confused elderly person with dementia wanders to the wrong house.

These are not hypotheticals. These are headlines. These are names. These are people who were shot, beaten, or killed because someone decided that the mere possibility of a property crime was worth a violent response.

Ralph Yarl, sixteen years old, shot through a door for ringing the wrong doorbell. Kaylin Gillis, shot for pulling into the wrong driveway. Are these the outcomes we want to defend? Is this the society we want to build?

When we say "violence to protect property is justified," we are handing a loaded philosophical weapon to every frightened, angry, or impulsive person and saying, "Your things are worth more than your judgment needs to be careful."

But I want to go deeper than consequences. I want to talk about what this belief does to our souls.

When we elevate property to the level where its defense warrants harm to human beings, we are making a declaration about our values. We are saying that our relationship with our things matters more than our relationship with our shared humanity.

Think about that. Really think about it.

What does it do to a person to take a life over a stolen car and then have to live with that forever? What does it do to a child who watches their parent shoot someone over a break-in, and grows up believing that this is proportional, that this is justice?

We become harder. We become more suspicious. We become people who see threats instead of neighbors, enemies instead of strangers, and targets instead of human beings. We begin to want the confrontation. We begin to fantasize about it. We begin to see our property not as things we enjoy but as territory we must be willing to kill to keep.

Is that freedom? Or is that a prison of our own making?

The great moral traditions of human civilization — virtually all of them — draw a clear line here.

They tell us that human life possesses a dignity that objects do not and cannot possess. They tell us that mercy is not weakness. They tell us that restraint in the face of provocation is not cowardice but courage — perhaps the highest form of courage there is.

It takes no courage to pull a trigger over a stolen television. It takes immense courage to say, "That is my property, and I want it back, but I will not destroy a human being to keep it. I will pursue justice through means that do not require me to become something less than what I am."

And let us talk about justice, because that word gets misused in these conversations constantly.

Justice is not the same as vengeance. Justice is not the same as retribution in the moment. Justice is a system — imperfect, yes, but a system — designed to weigh evidence, consider context, and impose proportional consequences.

When an individual uses violence to protect property, they are not dispensing justice. They are bypassing it. They are saying, "I don't trust the system, so I will be the system." But a system of one, acting in anger and fear, with no accountability and no deliberation, is not justice. It is chaos wearing the mask of order.

Let me tell you what I believe — truly, deeply believe.

I believe that a society's greatness is not measured by how fiercely its citizens guard their possessions. It is measured by how it treats its most vulnerable, its most desperate, and yes, even its most wayward members.

I believe that every time we choose restraint over violence, dialogue over destruction, and human dignity over material attachment, we build something more valuable than anything we could ever own.

I believe that your property matters — but not more than your humanity. Not more than your capacity for mercy. And not more than the basic, irreducible truth that a human life, any human life, cannot be weighed against an object and found wanting.

So what do I ask of you?

I ask you to protect your property — wisely, prudently, through every nonviolent means available to you.

I ask you to defend your life and your family's life with everything you have, should they truly be in danger.

But I ask you to refuse — firmly, courageously, and with moral clarity — to accept the proposition that your things, your stuff, your possessions are reason enough to do violence to another human being.

Because the moment we accept that proposition, we have already lost something far more valuable than anything that could ever be stolen from us.

We have lost our claim to be civilized. We have lost our moral bearings. And we have lost sight of the simple, radical, world-changing truth that people matter more than things.

Always.

Thank you.

The Injustice of Violence in Defense of Private Property

In societies across the globe, the notion of private property is deeply ingrained, serving as a cornerstone of economic systems and individual livelihoods. However, when this protection extends to the use of violence, ethical and moral questions arise. Is it justified to employ violence solely to defend private property from theft? This essay argues that using violence in such circumstances is not justified, as the defense of property alone is insufficient to warrant violent actions. This stance is grounded in ethical considerations, the value of human life over material possessions, legal principles, and the societal implications of endorsing violence for property defense.

Ethical Considerations and the Sanctity of Human Life

At the heart of this argument lies the ethical principle that human life holds a higher intrinsic value than material property. Philosophical doctrines such as Kantian ethics emphasize the inherent worth of individuals, advocating that people should be treated as ends in themselves, not merely as means to an end. Employing violence against a person to protect property reduces the individual's value to that of the objects being protected, undermining their inherent human dignity.

Utilitarian ethics, which focuses on the greatest good for the greatest number, also challenges the justification of violence in property defense. The harm inflicted on the thief—potentially severe injury or death—may far outweigh the benefit of retaining the property. This disproportionate outcome suggests that non-violent means of addressing theft are ethically preferable, minimizing harm while still respecting property rights.

Legal Principles and Proportionality of Force

Legally, many jurisdictions recognize the principle of proportionality in self-defense and defense of property. The use of force must be reasonable and commensurate with the threat faced. Lethal or severe force is generally considered acceptable only when there is an imminent threat to one's life or the lives of others, not merely to protect possessions.

For example, the European Court of Human Rights has emphasized that deprivation of life cannot be justified solely for the protection of property. Similarly, in the United States, while laws vary by state, the use of deadly force is commonly restricted to scenarios where there is a reasonable perception of a significant threat to personal safety. These legal frameworks reflect a societal consensus that human life and wellbeing take precedence over material goods.

The Potential for Escalation and Unintended Consequences

Utilizing violence to defend property introduces the risk of escalating conflicts, potentially leading to more severe harm than the initial threat posed by the theft. An attempt to deter theft through violent means can provoke retaliation, endangering not only the property owner but also bystanders and the broader community. This escalation undermines social stability and can contribute to cycles of violence.

Furthermore, the use of violence may have unintended legal and personal consequences for the property owner. Legal repercussions can include criminal charges, civil liabilities, and long-term harm to one's reputation and mental health. These outcomes often far exceed the value of the property initially at risk, questioning the prudence of choosing a violent response.

Alternative Non-Violent Measures for Property Protection

There are numerous non-violent strategies available to protect private property that do not involve the ethical and legal pitfalls associated with violence. Preventative measures, such as installing security systems, using locks, and increasing surveillance, can deter potential thieves without direct confrontation.

In the event of theft, legal avenues provide mechanisms for restitution and justice. Reporting crimes to law enforcement allows for the possibility of recovering stolen property and holding perpetrators accountable within the bounds of the law. Relying on these systems respects the rule of law and reduces the risk of harm to all parties involved.

Societal Implications and the Erosion of Social Norms

Endorsing violence for the defense of property can have detrimental effects on societal norms and values. It may foster a culture where material possessions are valued over human life, eroding the moral fabric that holds communities together. This shift can lead to increased violence overall, as individuals may feel justified in using force for personal gain or protection.

Societies function best when there is a collective agreement on the sanctity of life and the appropriate means of resolving conflicts. Upholding these principles promotes trust, cooperation, and the peaceful coexistence necessary for a stable and prosperous community.

Individuals bear a moral responsibility to minimize harm in their interactions with others. Resorting to violence absent a direct threat to personal safety contradicts this responsibility. By choosing non-violent responses to theft, individuals contribute to a more ethical and compassionate society.

Moreover, recognizing the potential social and economic factors that contribute to theft can inspire efforts to address underlying issues such as poverty, inequality, and lack of opportunity. Such approaches can reduce crime rates more effectively than individual acts of violent defense.

Conclusion

While the protection of private property is an important aspect of personal and economic security, it does not justify the use of violence. Ethical principles prioritize human life and wellbeing above material possessions, and legal systems generally prohibit disproportionate force in defense of property. Violence introduces risks of escalation, legal consequences, and societal harm that outweigh the benefits of protecting property through such means. By embracing non-violent strategies and addressing broader social issues, individuals and societies can safeguard property rights while upholding the values of human dignity and the sanctity of life.
